Chapter 5: Power and Knowledge — How Definitions Shape Control.
There’s this quiet force that slips into every rulebook, every diagnosis, every test score. It’s not loud, but it’s always there—the power to define what’s normal, what’s healthy, what’s considered good. And here’s the thing: this power doesn’t come from laws or police. It comes from knowledge. From the experts and institutions that decide how people are measured—and judged.
Picture a student, sitting in front of a test. Pencil in hand, heart pounding. Those questions? They aren’t just about facts. They’re about what matters. What’s valued. What’s even possible. That score? It’s going to shape this student’s future—open some doors, close others. So, the test isn’t just a measure. It’s a tool of power.
Or think about a patient in a doctor’s office, waiting for a diagnosis. The doctor’s words carry real weight—not just because of all that training, but because those words define what counts as illness, what needs to be treated, and what can be ignored. That diagnosis shapes how the patient sees themselves, how others treat them, and what options they actually have.
In every institution, knowledge and power are tangled up together. The experts who set the rules? They’re also the ones who enforce them. The categories they create—like normal and abnormal, healthy and sick, good and bad—they become the basis for discipline and control.
Most folks trust the experts, thinking that knowledge is neutral, objective, and fair. But here’s something to pay attention to: knowledge is always shaped by power—by the interests, values, and goals of those who produce it. The categories used to sort people aren’t natural. They’re made. And they serve certain purposes.
Now, this doesn’t mean knowledge is false or useless. It just means that knowledge is always part of a bigger system of power—always connected to the ways people are controlled and shaped.
The real power of knowledge? It’s in its ability to make certain ways of thinking feel natural, inevitable, and just plain right. It tells us what counts as a problem, what needs fixing, and—maybe most importantly—who gets to decide.
